newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia plans on five pct annual GDP growth by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Russia plans on five pct annual GDP growth by 2000.

text.p: The Russian cabinet gave its backing on Thursday to a blueprint for economic development which foresees output growth of five percent a year by 2000, Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said.
"It is an exceptionally difficult task, but we cannot do it any other way," Yasin told a news conference.
Russia's economy, as measured by gross domestic product, shrank by six percent in the first nine months of this year and Yasin has previously forecast a five percent GDP fall in 1996.
Officials have been predicting a return to growth in Russia for years but it has yet to materialise.
President Boris Yeltsin said after he was re-elected in July that the main economic goal was to revive production.

The new programme foresees a two percent budget deficit, annual inflation of five to eight percent and a rise in foreign investment to at least $10-12 billion by 2000, Yasin said, adding foreign investment this year would be $3.5-$4 billion.
He has previously forecast 1996 inflation of 23-25 percent.
"It is a very difficult programme," Yasin said. "The main goal is renewal of economic growth."

The plan forecasts a fall in commercial banks' refinancing rates to between three and five percent above inflation and a fall in Treasury bill yields to 15 percent above inflation from the current 50 percent, he said.
After winning cabinet approval for the programme, the economy ministry will start working out how to implement it.

Changes it wants to introduce include a shift to international accounting standards for Russian firms, higher gas and electricity prices for households but lower prices for industry, more independent share registers and timely tax payments, he said.
A shortfall in tax collection is one of the most serious economic problems in Russia.
The International Monetary Fund last month delayed payment of the next tranche of its $10 billion loan to Russia.
An IMF mission is currently working in Moscow to assess whether to issue the tranche.
Yasin said tax revenues in November were better than in October but were still too low.
